notes:
I could only research part of this. My tool limit ran out after one source, the Enduring Word commentary by David Guzik. That page cut off partway through, so I have notes only on **vv. 1–16**. I found nothing on vv. 17–40, nothing on how Protestant traditions differ (part 2), and nothing on modern scholarship, Catholic, Orthodox or popular modern readings (part 3). Following your rules, I've left those out rather than filling them in from memory.

Guzik comments on the NKJV, so his wording sometimes differs from the BSB. Where he quotes older writers (Hodge, Clarke, Calvin, Morris, Trapp, Barclay), I say so. Those are his quotations; I haven't read the original works.

**Source for every note below:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-7/

---

**v. 1:** This verse starts a new section where Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him by letter. Guzik reads "not to touch a woman" (BSB "abstain from sexual relations") as meaning sex. He thinks it was probably the Corinthians' own slogan, and Paul agrees with it only partly. The "nevertheless" of v. 2 is the limit he puts on it. Guzik suggests some Corinthians thought giving up sex entirely, even within marriage, would make them purer, because sexual sin was such a danger. He quotes Hodge: seeing marriage as less holy than celibacy led people to think married couples should separate.

**v. 2:** Because sexual immorality was everywhere, husband and wife should "have" each other sexually. Guzik says this is not an order to get married. It is an order for married people to keep living as married people, including continuing sexual relations. He adds that Paul is not saying sex is the only or main reason for marriage. Paul is answering a specific question, not giving a full theology of marriage; for that, Guzik points to Ephesians 5 and Colossians 3. He quotes Clarke's warning against spouses who think they are "too holy" to keep this command.

**v. 3:** The duty runs both ways, and the stress is on giving ("I owe you"), not on demanding ("you owe me"). The NKJV wording, "the affection due her," shows that every Christian wife is owed affection, not just sex. Guzik says couples who cannot have a full sexual relationship can still keep this command through affection.

**v. 4:** The obligation is so real that each spouse's body can be said to belong to the other. Guzik says plainly that this does not justify a husband abusing or coercing his wife. The point is that each spouse is bound to serve the other with physical affection, and that God has given each person one partner only.

**v. 5:** Paul rejects the idea that married couples become holier by giving up sex. Guzik notes that the word for "deprive" is the same one translated "defraud" in 6:8, so withholding intimacy cheats the spouse. Deprivation can mean a lack of romance as well as infrequent sex, and either kind can push the deprived spouse to look elsewhere. Guzik turns "lack of self-control" around: refusing sex is what shows a lack of self-control, and it opens the door to Satan's temptation. He says Satan's strategy is both to encourage sex outside marriage and to discourage it inside marriage.

**v. 6:** The "concession" is the brief break for prayer and fasting. God allows it reluctantly, but he does not command or even recommend it, and the couple must come back together afterwards.

**v. 7:** Guzik says Paul was unmarried when he wrote this, but had probably been married before. His reasons: observant Jews treated marriage as a duty, and Acts 26:10 suggests Paul voted as a member of the Sanhedrin, which unmarried men could not join. Scripture does not say what happened to his wife. Guzik stresses that Paul calls both marriage and singleness gifts from God. The Greek word for "gift" is the same one used for spiritual gifts in chapter 12. He also says no one is "gifted" for sexual immorality. Guzik quotes Trapp, and Clarke citing the Gemara, to show that Jews treated staying unmarried as sinful, which makes Paul's view of singleness all the more striking.

**v. 8:** Paul counts himself among "the unmarried and widows" and sees real advantages in staying single. Guzik says Paul explains these later in the chapter, on practical grounds.

**v. 9:** Paul's advice to marry is practical, not a claim that marriage is more or less spiritual than singleness. Guzik connects this to 1 Timothy 4:1–3, where forbidding marriage is called a doctrine of demons. Quoting Calvin, he says "burn" means being overwhelmed by passion, not ordinary temptation. He also warns that marriage does not by itself cure lust.

**vv. 10–11:** Paul is speaking to marriages where both spouses are believers. Some Corinthians asked whether breaking up a marriage would make them holier, and Paul passes on the Lord's own answer: no. Guzik holds that God accepts only two grounds for divorce: sexual immorality (Matthew 19:3–9) and an unbelieving spouse deserting a believer (v. 15). Anyone who divorces on other grounds is not free to remarry and can only be reconciled. Guzik grants that separating might sometimes be justified, for example in cases of abuse or addiction. But the separated spouses are still married in God's eyes, "separate, but not single." He notes that Jesus permitted divorce for adultery but never commanded it.

**v. 12:** Guzik says "I, not the Lord" does not make this teaching any less inspired. It only means Jesus had not spoken to this particular case, so his apostle does. He suggests Paul may not have known how fully inspired he was as he wrote. Being married to an unbeliever is not a reason to end the marriage. Guzik notes that 2 Corinthians 6:14 is a reason not to marry an unbeliever in the first place, which is a different matter.

**v. 13:** The same rule applies to a believing wife with an unbelieving husband who is willing to stay. She must not divorce him.

**v. 14:** "Sanctified" does not mean the unbelieving spouse is saved by being married to a believer. It means they are set apart for the Holy Spirit's work because they live so close to a Christian. On "holy" children, Guzik quotes Morris: until a child is old enough to take responsibility, the child of a believer should be regarded as Christian. Guzik's own view is that such children are saved until they reach an age of accountability. He says the text gives no similar assurance for children of non-Christian parents. If any of those children go to heaven, it is through God's mercy, not because they are innocent. This is a contested reading, and I could not check how other traditions handle the verse.

**v. 15:** The believer must not start the break-up. But if the unbeliever refuses to stay in the marriage, the believer is "not under bondage." Guzik takes this to mean the divorce is valid in God's eyes and the believer is free to remarry.

**v. 16:** Guzik reads this verse as hope for believers married to unbelievers: with faith and patience, God may work in the situation. He adds 1 Peter 3:1–6, where it is godly conduct more than words that wins the spouse. He also quotes Barclay: an early pagan complaint against Christians was that they broke up families.
